div.head: Schedulability analysis of real-time system has been a
div.p: central focus of research in scheduling theory and a remarkable progress is made in recent years. This progress provides the opportunity to integrate these state of the art results into real-time networks, so that the analysis time for the feasibility of periodic messages is reduced. In this paper, we employ such advancement in the widely studied IEEE 802.5 protocol for scheduling real-time packets. Our technique avoids false points, the point (time) at which a particular packet is not schedulable, that arise during feasibility analysis and eventually the analysis is done more efficiently.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In contrast to CSMA/CD networks such as Ethernet, tokenpassing networks are deterministic [2]; it is possible to determine the maximum time that will be passed before any end station is capable of transmitting. From real-time traffic perspective, Token-Ring/IEEE 802.5 networks has several advantages such as supporting prioritized scheduling of packets and detecting/overcoming the network faults. This paper particulary addresses IEEE 802.5 which is the choice for real-time systems for applications that can run with a limited number of priority levels and have low data rate requirements.

It is a must to maintain the timing requirements of a packet for hard real-time applications running on IEEE 802.5 network. The most commonly suited timing constrain in real-time networks is deadline [13]: the packets has to reach from the source to destination in a fixed time interval.

For validating timing constrains, feasibility tests-given a task set and system model, determining whether it is possible to meet all the deadlines -are performed to achieve system predictability. Feasibility analysis in uniprocessor domain are attaining much focus recently and can be efficiently applied to the communication networks.

Since the classic paper of Liu and Layland [7], the scheduling theory is tailored for enormous applications and networks are no exception [11,3,12,10,1,4]. Stronsnider et al. applied scheduling theory for the first time to the IEEE 802.5 Token Ring for the hard real-time applications in [12]. Kamat and Zhao [3] compared the performance of priority driven and timed token protocols and concluded that priority driven performs better at low bandwidth (1 -10Mbps), while timed token has superior performance at higher bandwidth. Though efficient, the feasibility test provided in [3] has tendency for testing packet feasibility at redundant points. Recently, Min-Allah et al. discussed fixed priority techniques in [9] which provides better result than existing schemes. Extending the work in [3,12,9], we apply state of the art results for the analysis of period packets scheduled on the IEEE 802.5 local area network protocol.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We discuss necessary back ground in Section 2 while the system model is provided in Section 3. Section 4 describes the IEEE 802.5 in detail. The main result of this paper is presented in Section 5, where we derive a novel algorithm to determine the feasibility of periodically released packets in a graceful way. Finally, we conclude the paper in Section 6.

div.head: Preliminaries
div.p: The problem of scheduling periodic task under fixedpriority scheme was first addressed by Liu and Layland [7] in 1973 under simplified assumptions (for details see [7] ), they derived the optimal static priority scheduling algorithm for period task model (when deadlines coincide with respective periods) called rate monotonic (RM) algorithm. RM assigns static priorities on task activation rates (periods) such 978-1-4244-1980-7/08/$25.00 ©2008 IEEE.

div.head: System Model
div.p: Let M = {M 1 , M 2 , ...M 3 } denotes a set of synchronous periodic messages in a distributed system. Each message M i is described by its execution time C i associated with sending a message, its period P i , its maximum blocking time B i and deadline D i . In contrast to scheduling period tasks , scheduling packets for transmission is different in three respects. (1) The packet is re-transmitted once it is preempted by a higher priority packet during its transmission.

(2) In addition to transmitting actual message, header, source/destination addresses and other information is also associated with it (See Figure 1). (3) Since the system is distributed, decisions as to which packet has the highest priority may be made on the basis of outdate information. For detailed understanding of theses issues, interested reader is referred to [5]. In IEEE 802.5 token ring network, packets are transmitted in one direction along a circular transmission medium. A station transmits a packet by breaking the network and placing its packets on the output link to the network. As the packet circulates around the network, the station(s) identified by the network destination address in the packet header copies the packet. When the packet returns to the source station, the station removes the packet from the network. We use the term messages and packet interchangeably in rest of the paper.

div.head: IEEE 802.5 token ring basics
div.p: In this section, we briefly describe the IEEE 802.5 token ring basics in Figure 1 . The length of a field is mentioned in bits for access control, while the respective length of each field for data packet is shown in bytes.

div.head: Token Format
div.p: • Start delimiter: Alerts each station of the arrival of a token (or data/command frame). This field includes signals that distinguish the byte from the rest of the frame by violating the encoding scheme used elsewhere in the frame.

• Access control: Contains the priority field and the reservation field, as well as a token bit (used to differentiate a token from a data/command frame) and a monitor bit (used by the active monitor to determine whether a frame is circling the ring endlessly).
• End delimiter: Signals the end of the token or data/command frame. This field also contains bits to indicate a damaged frame and identify the frame that is the last in a logical sequence.

div.head: Data/ Frame Fields
div.p: Since the Start-delimiter, Access-control and End-delimiter are discussed above, we describe the remaining fields here:
• Frame control: Indicates whether the frame contains data or control information. In control frames, this byte specifies the type of control information.
• Destination and source addresses : consists of two 6-byte address fields that identify the destination and source station addresses.
• Data : indicates that the length of field is limited by the ring token holding time, which defines the maximum time a station can hold the token.
Figure 1: Token, data packet and address control format

• Frame check sequence: Is filed by the source station with a calculated value dependent on the frame contents. The destination station recalculates the value to determine whether the frame was damaged in transit.
If so, the frame is discarded.
• Frame Status: Terminates a data frame. The Frame Status field includes the address-recognized indicator and frame-copied indicator.
The role of access control filed is important from scheduling point of view while, frame status field result in reliable transmission.

div.head: Message priority arbitration
div.p: Priority based scheduling of packet is achieved by a simple mechanism through address control filed. In particularly, the first three bits (the most significant bits) of the field represent the token priority while the last three bits (the least significant bits) contain the reservation priority. The token is only seized by a node n i when its outgoing packet has an equal of higher priority than the current priority. Once the token is seized by a node, first, it keeps the token priority unchanged but puts the reservation priority to the lowest priority of the network and secondly, it marks the token busy and puts the token in the header of the packet and transmits the packet. Reservation for the next turn to use the network is done distributedly during the transmission of a data packet. As a data circulates around the ring, a station with outgoing packets can make a reservation for future use of a network by setting the reservation priority bits in the access control to the highest priority of its outgoing packets. When the data packet returns to the source station, the reservation priority is equal to the highest priority of all packets waiting at all stations to be transmitted on the network.

div.head: Reliable Message Delivery
div.p: Once the message is delivered from source to destination, the source node is notified by the the value of frame control field. Specifically, a logical False-False combination means the failure of the destination such as it is down or encountered some fault. The False-True value says that the destination is available but the message was not copied by the destination. A True-True mechanism confirms the successfully delivery of packet to the destination.

Theorem 5 -Given a set of n periodic packets {M 1 , ..., M n } scheduled by RM, every false feasibility point for M i on a token ring network for all packet phasings is also a false feasibility point for packet having priority lower than M i .

div.head: Definition 3 (Set of False Feasibility Points)
div.p: A false feasibility point T for a packet M i , in a token ring network, becomes chained point for the packet with priority lower than M i . We represent all the false feasibility points contributed by M i with a set X i such that X i becomes a set of false feasibility points for {M i+1 , ...M n }.

Proof. From Theorem 4, we known that, if T is a false feasibility point for M i-1 then it must also be a false feasibility point for M i . Consequently to calculate L i , we confined our search to a reduced set Z i ⊆ S i , by excluding set of chained points.

We have replaced S i given in Theorem 2 by Z i , which immediately reflects the reduced complexity of our technique Z i ⊆ S i ; allows us to search reduced number of inequalities for determining packet feasibility, which is the main contribution of this paper.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Feasibility analysis of preemptive uniprocessors is well understood and applied to numerous fields. Since the computer network is no exception, the fundamental issue of feasibility analysis of real-time systems is addressed from IEEE 802.5 token ring perspective. The latest results from fixed priority scheduling theory are applied so that the timing constraints of packets are checked in a descent way while keeping the under lying assumptions unchanged. Mathematical proofs provide the correctness of our results and the advantage is clear form testing packet feasibility at reduced number of points as compared to existing alternatives.
